item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable

Good morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. When he stepped down in the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party.

But the Cockroach protests that have swept through India this summer are about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the past 12 years. They’re also a lesson in using humour to political advantage.

Wild fires | Authorities in France battled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency.

Germany | A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said.

Iran | The US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.

UK politics | Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank.

UK news | Five Palestine Action activists face being sentenced as terrorists for breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire.

Monday | Andrew and Tristan Tate are due back in the Florida court where they’re fighting their extradition to the UK, to face rape and sex-trafficking charges.

Tuesday | Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are expected to be among those attending the Washington DC memorial service for the late South Carolina senator and Trump ally Lindsey Graham.

Thursday | People will go to the polls to elect the next mayor of Greater Manchester, who will replace Andy Burnham.

“The sky changed colour. It seemed like a cloud but it was smoke covering the sun – it wasn’t a natural phenomenon. It didn’t seem real,” said Nassir, an English literature graduate from Kabul who has been living in France for seven years. “We couldn’t breathe easily, you could feel it in your lungs.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US Senator Graham offered military support for Israeli war on Lebanon, new footage shows
item.description:
US Senator Graham offered military support for Israeli war on Lebanon, new footage shows

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 07/27/2026 - 18:51
A loud and proud interventionist, Lindsey Graham's funeral is scheduled for Tuesday
Former US Senator Lindsey Graham waves to reporters after his meeting with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv, Ukraine on 10 July 2026 (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)
Off

Just one day before his funeral is set to take place in Washington, DC, video footage has emerged showing a gleeful Senator Lindsey Graham rejoicing at the launch of the US-Israeli war on Iran, and even single-handedly offering US military involvement to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for his war on Lebanon.

The clips are from British filmmaker Alex Holder, who has been following Graham for the last three years for a documentary on his relationship with President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. 

Holder appears to have been granted access to staff meetings on Capitol Hill as well as discussions Graham had with national and foreign leaders, including the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday. 

"I almost cried. How long have we been pushing this?" Graham is seen asking members of his office in one clip, as he watched Trump give remarks to the press five days into the launch of the war on Iran.

"[Trump] loves blowing stuff up," Graham said.

"There are a lot of people inside that didn't want to do it. So I've had my challenges. President Trump, when he gets into the zone, he listens, asks good questions. You know, no tweeting... He's been a great wartime president," he added. 

"I said last last night that Trump and Bibi are like Roosevelt and Churchill. I mean, they're the right two guys to to confront this evil."

In another clip, Graham is again seen in his office, having dialed Netanyahu and put him on speakerphone.

"I'm just so impressed. Glad to be your friend," he began the call. 

"I'm going to meet with the president this weekend. I'm going down to Doral," he said, referencing Trump's golf club in Florida. 

"I'm going to try to get him to join with y'all in Lebanon to maybe fly some with you. Would you like that?" Graham asked, in a stunning unilateral offer for US military intervention in Lebanon, where Israel had significantly escalated its air and ground assault along with its attacks on Iran. 

"Yeah, I I get that. I think I think you have a point, but I've been thinking about the other side of it for a second. We're concentrating right now on Iran," Netanyahu responded.

Lindsey Graham, staunch backer of Israel and US wars, dies aged 71
Read More »

"If we tell Hezbollah that we're going all the way, we're threatening them. But if we actually do it, okay, then they have no reason not to go all the way against us, okay. That's not our interest."

Graham replied that he only "put it out there as an idea", and that he appreciated Netanyahu's "good counsel".

A third clip from the documentary showed Graham on the phone while in the passenger seat of a moving vehicle, speaking to former White House national security adviser Jake Sullivan.

"To be honest with you, I think about three to four weeks we should have them in a spot where they start losing control of some cities," Graham said on the call in reference to Iran.

"And what we're trying to do is just get a few cities to fall in the next month. Get the Arabs more openly involved tomorrow, or by the end of the week, and just have almost irreversible momentum."

Five months in, that momentum still has not materialised. 

'Conflicted'

The Wall Street Journal detailed some conversations from clips not yet publicly available, including further discussion with Sullivan in which Graham complains that Trump's chief negotiators - his peace envoy Steve Witkoff, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner - are simply not equipped to handle talks on Gaza or Iran. 

“I can’t do it with Jared, and I can’t do it with Witkoff. They’re just too conflicted. It’s gotta be Rubio," Graham reportedly said.

Holder told the Wall Street Journal that Graham was closer to Saudi Arabia's Mohamed Bin Salman than any other US official, and that Graham was also treated like a king whenever he went to Israel to meet with Netanyahu or the Mossad.

The senator is said to have frequently complained that many people inside the administration and surrounding Trump are against the war on Iran and angling for a deal, which complicated Graham's endeavours.

“Very few people are out selling this war from the administration. I’m shocked,” he reportedly said.

But he also relished how much media attention he was getting since the war - which he had been demanding for decades - kicked off. 

“We could do a media show every two seconds," Graham told the documentary crew. 

Forever interventionist

Long one of the loudest voices on US foreign policy and a loyal ally to Trump, Graham died suddenly at the age of 71 from an aortic dissection earlier this month. 

First elected to the Senate in 2002, Graham regularly courted intense international criticism for his pro-war rhetoric and interventionist foreign policy. 

Karim Khan describes threats from David Cameron and Lindsey Graham in new interview
Read More »

He staunchly backed Israel in the US Congress and called for increased military assistance to Tel Aviv alongside increased aid for illegal settlements. 

Netanyahu characterised him as a close friend of Israel, while President Isaac Herzog declared Graham's support for the country had been unwavering.

Throughout Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, Graham repeatedly defended Israeli military actions and opposed efforts to restrict US support for Israel.

His comments frequently drew criticism from Palestinian rights advocates, human rights groups and Muslim civil rights organisations.

In July 2024, Graham described Palestinians in Gaza as "the most radicalized population on the planet who are taught to hate Jews from birth" in a social media post that sparked widespread condemnation.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations responded by saying that he was promoting racist stereotypes about Palestinians, calling his comments "hateful and absurd". 

Graham also drew flak for suggesting that Israel should consider measures comparable to those used by the United States against Japan during World War Two, remarks that opponents described as inflammatory.

In 2019, during a visit to the occupied Golan Heights, Graham called Israel's security and prosperity vital to US national security and advocated recognition of Israeli control over the territory.

In March, he blamed Saudi Arabia for refusing to join the US-Israeli war against Iran and warned of potential "consequences" for countries that declined to support military action against Tehran.

item.description:
Palestinian woman delivers stillborn baby after Israeli checkpoint delay, medics say

Palestinian health workers said a woman delivered a stillborn baby in an ambulance after the vehicle was reportedly delayed by Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint in the occupied West Bank on Monday, AFP reported on Monday.

The 28-year-old woman was six months pregnant and unconscious when medics collected her from her home in the village of Qaryout, south of the city of Nablus, medic Bashar Qaryouti told AFP.

"She was suffering from very heavy bleeding and her condition was extremely critical," Qaryouti said, adding that the ambulance was heading to Rafidia hospital in Nablus via Awarta checkpoint, where the Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance.

He said Israeli soldiers at the checkpoint forced him to switch off the ambulance at gunpoint despite him explaning that the vehicle's medical equipment was being used to keep a patient alive. A nurse accompanying her was forced delivering the stillborn baby.

The bleeding woman was rushed to the hospital after waiting at the checkpoint over 30 minutes and is now in stable condition, report said. 

Reporting by AFP

Just one in three Americans support the war on Iran, the lowest reading in a Reuters/Ipsos poll since the five-month-old conflict's early days, with most respondents saying that President Donald Trump has failed to explain his goals.

The poll, conducted Friday through Sunday, also showed the Republican president's approval rating ticking higher to 37 percent, up three points from last month when his rating tied the lowest of his presidency.

The poll found that 69 percent of Americans, including four in 10 Republicans, think Trump has not "clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran."

Approval of the conflict has been below 40 percent since the US and Israel launched strikes on 28 February - a stark contrast to the opening months of other recent conflicts.

While each had different context, the Iraq War from 2003 to 2011 had the support of about 70 percent of Americans in its early months. During the early days of the Afghanistan War, which lasted from 2001 to 2021, about 90 percent of the country backed the war, according to polling by Gallup.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Cottage pie and glass of red, anyone? Britons shun salad despite heat in ‘reverse comfort eating’
item.description:
Nostalgic foods like toad-in-the-hole also in demand at Waitrose as people pivot towards familiarity amid climatic and political upheaval

Forget a crisp salad and glass of chilled rosé. Enervated Britons are seemingly more likely to crave a rich cottage pie and a robust red in heatwaves.

In a trend termed “reverse comfort eating”, Waitrose’s cottage pie sales have soared 110% in the last month and South African red wine is up 68% compared with the same period last year. The surprise spike in demand for winter comfort foods also includes retro chicken, bacon and leek pie (up 41%), chicken korma (up 67%) and chicken and ham gratin (68%).

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] World-class Jodrell Bank is under threat and UK risks a physics brain drain
item.description:
Funding crisis could lead to an exodus that would be a blow for British science and national growth

On a chilly day in December 1945, Bernard Lovell, a physicist at the University of Manchester, struck out for the Cheshire countryside to study cosmic rays, the streams of high-energy particles that crisscross the universe. Peering at the signals from his army surplus radar, he made an unexpected discovery: radio reflections from the ionised trails of shooting stars.

The work marked the birth of radio astronomy at Jodrell Bank. A year later, engineers at the site mounted a radar on the base of a searchlight, providing sweeping access to speeding meteors. When Sputnik launched in 1957, they had just completed the Lovell telescope, the largest radio telescope in the world, the only one capable of tracking the Soviet satellite.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Australia news live: new Victorian premier Ben Carroll announces construction royal commission; Angus Taylor donations raised in Icac
item.description:
Follow updates live

  • Jacinta Allan resigns as Victorian premier before leadership challenge by Ben Carroll

  • Who is Ben Carroll?

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

ACTU president says now is the ‘right time’ to leave

Michele O’Neil, the president of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, said it’s the “right time” to leave after she announced her departure alongside ACTU secretary Sally McManus.

We thought about this and we just think that it’s time for renewal. The union movement is in good shape. We’ve seen changes in workers’ rights that have made a big difference in workers’ lives. We’ve seen the union movement starting to grow for the first time in decades. And next year will be the 100th anniversary of the ACTU. So we think it’s time for a new leadership team to come in.

We have a debt heading towards $200bn in this state. We have teachers out striking in the streets because the state government and Ben Carroll can’t secure a pay deal. We have holes in the roads. You need a majority government to fix those problems, and you need someone with a plan.

Now he might performatively call a royal commission tokenistically, now that he’s become leader, but that’s not out of sincere concern about corruption. That’s out of sincere concern about the polls and what that means for Victorian Labor.
